opus-5.5.text:
I think Cosmos is quite central to how Nvidia thinks about the next wave of AI. If you look at the history, the first big wave was perception — recognizing images, speech. Then we had the generative AI wave with large language models, which is really about digital intelligence: text, code, images. But the next frontier, in our view, is physical AI — AI that can perceive, reason, and act in the physical world. Robots, autonomous vehicles, smart factories, and so on.

The problem is that physical AI faces a data bottleneck that language models don't have in the same way. For language, you have the internet, decades of text people have written. For robots, you don't have an internet-scale dataset of robot interactions. Collecting real-world data is expensive, slow, and sometimes dangerous — you can't crash a car a thousand times to learn about edge cases.

So Cosmos is our answer to that. It's a world foundation model platform — models that understand how the world evolves, physics, cause and effect, and can generate plausible future states given actions. Developers can use it as a simulator, as a data generator, as a policy evaluator, or even as a starting point to build their own policy models. We see it as the foundation that the physical AI ecosystem can build on.

Within Nvidia's overall model strategy, we have Nemotron on the language and reasoning side, and things like GR00T for humanoid robots, and Cosmos sits underneath as the world model layer. And importantly, we made it open — open weights, a permissive license — because we believe physical AI is still early, and the field needs a common foundation. Nvidia's mission has always been to enable the whole ecosystem. If many companies can build great robots and AVs faster, that's good for everyone, and of course it also drives demand for accelerated computing, from training in the data center to simulation in Omniverse to deployment on Jetson and Thor at the edge.

So I'd say Cosmos is not a side project. It's one of the key pillars of how we want to make physical AI happen.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes perception, generative AI, and Physical AI, but does not identify Agentic AI and Physical AI as the two main categories of Nvidia’s model strategy.

r002.rationale: It calls Cosmos the world-model layer beneath models such as GR00T and says developers can use it as a starting point for their own policy models, conveying that other Physical AI models are built from it.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe Nvidia’s internal autonomous-vehicle or robotics teams as customers of the Cosmos team.

r004.rationale: It presents Physical AI as the next frontier after generative AI, but does not say that current competition focuses on Agentic AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the simplest way to put it is that Cosmos is how Nvidia tries to bring the kind of progress we've seen in language models to the physical world.

If you look at the last few years, LLMs got extraordinarily good because there was an enormous amount of text on the internet to learn from. Physical AI, robots, autonomous vehicles, machines that have to perceive and act in the real world, doesn't have that luxury. You cannot scrape the internet and get a trillion examples of a robot arm picking up a cup in a kitchen with the lighting slightly different. Collecting that data physically is slow, expensive, and sometimes dangerous. So the bottleneck for physical AI is not really the model architecture, it's data and the simulation of the world.

Cosmos is our answer to that. It's a family of world foundation models, models that understand physics, understand how a scene evolves over time, and can generate video of what happens next given a state and an action. That lets you do a few things. You can generate huge amounts of synthetic training data that's grounded in physics rather than just looking pretty. You can use the model as a simulator to test a policy before it ever touches a real robot. And you can use it as a foundation that developers fine-tune for their own robots, their own cars, their own factories.

Within Nvidia's strategy, I'd say it sits in the middle of a three-computer story. There's the computer you train on, the computer the robot runs on, and the computer that simulates the world in between, which is Omniverse plus Cosmos. Omniverse gives you the controllable, physically accurate scene; Cosmos gives you the learned generative model that can fill in the realism and the variety at scale. Together they're meant to close the gap between simulation and reality.

And we made it open, with open weights, because we genuinely think physical AI is too big for any single company to solve alone. The way I see it, Cosmos is less a product and more a platform, the same way CUDA was a platform. If every robotics company in the world builds on top of it, that's the outcome we want.

r001.rationale: The response discusses Physical AI but does not identify Agentic AI as the other main category in Nvidia’s model strategy.

r002.rationale: It describes Cosmos as a foundation that developers can fine-tune for their own robots, cars, and factories.

r003.rationale: The response does not frame Nvidia’s internal autonomous-vehicle or robotics teams as customers of the Cosmos team.

r004.rationale: It does not present Physical AI as the next frontier after competition focused on Agentic AI.

astra-6.text:
I see Cosmos as a foundational part of Nvidia’s strategy for physical AI. A robot or an autonomous vehicle needs more than the ability to understand language—it needs to understand how the physical world changes and how its actions affect what happens next. That’s where world models become important.

Cosmos is about building that foundation: models that can represent and predict the world, and help developers create the data and simulations needed to train physical AI systems. It complements language models because reasoning about a task and understanding its physical consequences are closely connected.

So its importance goes beyond any single application. The goal is to give people developing robots and autonomous systems a common foundation they can adapt to their own problems.

r001.rationale: The response discusses Physical AI and says Cosmos complements language models, but it does not distinguish Agentic AI and Physical AI as the two main categories of Nvidia’s model strategy.

r002.rationale: It calls Cosmos a common foundation developers can adapt to their problems, but does not clearly say application-specific Physical AI models are specialized on top of that foundation.

r003.rationale: The response mentions developers of robots and autonomous systems, but does not frame Nvidia’s internal robotics and autonomous-vehicle teams as Cosmos’s customers.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe Agentic AI as the current focus of competition or Physical AI as the next frontier.

sol-6.1.text:
I see Cosmos as a foundation for physical AI. A language model helps a system understand and communicate, but a robot or an autonomous vehicle also needs to understand how the world changes when it takes an action. World models are an important part of that.

Within Nvidia’s model strategy, Cosmos connects models to simulation and, ultimately, to systems operating in the real world. You can use generated scenarios to help train and evaluate those systems, including situations that are difficult to collect in real life. That complements real-world data and gives us a way to develop physical AI more efficiently.
